speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill C-172, to amend the Canada Grain Act (offtrack elevator licensing).
Explain.

speechtext:
that Bill S-8, to amend the Trust Companies Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill proposes to make certain amendments to the Trust Companies Act, the act which governs the activities of federally incorporated trust companies in Canada. There are nine such companies presently active, but they transact close to one-third of the trust company business in this country.
The amendments before us have four principal purposes:	First, to provide certain

expansions in the investment powers of trust companies; second, to establish a better and more flexible system of controlling companies if they should get into financial difficulty; third, to extend the prohibitions against investments and loans where there may be a conflict of interests and, fourth, to establish a letters patent system of incorporating companies and amending existing charters.
Dealing with investment powers, Mr. Speaker, a number of changes are proposed principally for the purpose of bringing the investment powers of trust companies into line with those of insurance companies as provided in amendments made in 1965. Pursuant to these changes, trust companies will be permitted to make mortgage loans on the security of leasehold as well as freehold real estate, to make investments outside Canada in any country in which they are doing business, to make investments in real estate for the production of income that qualifies on the basis of an earnings test and to make investments in real estate for the production of income in larger parcels than is presently permitted.
They would also be enabled to invest or lend guaranteed trust funds at their own discretion up to a maximum of 7 per cent of these funds. This corresponds to the so-called "basket" provision available to life insurance companies. At present, the power to make mortgage loans is subject to a restriction that the amount of any mortgage cannot exceed 75 per cent of the value of the real estate unless the excess is insured through a government agency. An amendment would permit mortgages to be made in excess of the 75 per cent limit if the excess is insured through a policy of mortgage insurance issued by a registered insurance company. Other changes would effect an expansion of investment powers in certain minor respects, bringing them into line with the powers of insurance companies.
Trust companies would be granted authority to own subsidiary companies in certain circumstances, subject to terms and conditions specified by the Governor in Council. They would be empowered to own and operate as subsidiaries, trust companies incorporated outside of Canada, companies incorporated to establish and operate a mutual investment fund, mortgage loan companies, or companies engaged in any activity reasonably ancillary to that of a trust company.
The existing requirement for a minimum statutory margin on collateral loans would be removed and companies would be able to
December 12, 1969

exercise their own discretion with respect to the margin of collateral over the amount of the loan.
The existing prohibitions against making loans to officers or directors would be expanded to prohibit loans to or investments by any major shareholder and also loans to or investments in any other corporation if a director, officer or major shareholder had a significant interest in that other corporation.
With respect to proposed revisions in the system of supervision and control of trust companies, the present act enables the minister to impose conditions or limitations in the licence of a company which is subject to annual renewal. The act also requires the superintendent to report to the minister if he considers that the assets of the company are insufficient to justify its continuation in business and the minister has the authority to suspend or cancel the licence of the company. It is now proposed that some flexibility be introduced to give certain states of control short of factual cancellation of the licence. The proposals are similar to those included in the proposed amendment to the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act with which we will be dealing later.
[DOT] (12 noon)
They would require the Superintendent to report to the minister when he considers that a company is in weak financial condition, where it has exceeded its borrowing powers or where the assets in Canada are not sufficient to cover the liabilities in Canada. The minister could then take one or more of three steps: he could impose conditions in the company's licence; he could prescribe a time within which the company is to remedy the defect; or he could direct the Superintendent to take control of the company's assets.
In any ease where the Superintendent has control of a company's assets, the minister may request the Attorney General to apply to a Superior court for an order, or requiring the Superintendent to take control of a company for its rehabilitation, or he may request the Attorney General to apply for a court order to wind up the company under the Winding-up Act. The Superintendent would be empowered to assess other trust companies for the expenses involved in control of a company by him.
As further steps in the pattern of improved supervision and reporting, trust companies would be required to file quarterly statements to permit up-to-date information to be gathered as to their liquidity position, and also
Trust Companies Act
semi-annual statements showing the changes in investments and loans. A provision would be inserted requiring companies to maintain a liquidity reserve equal to 20 per cent of the guaranteed funds repayable on demand or repayable within 100 days. This reserve would have to be in the form of federal or provincial bonds or cash.
Now, we come to another important amendment. At present, trust companies are limited to accepting guaranteed trust funds which do not exceed in total 15 times their capital and surplus. The amendment would propose that this limit be raised to 20 times, subject to approval by the minister on specific application by a company. This amendment, like the one I have just mentioned in connection with the amount of mortgage a trust company can provide, will enable trust companies to make more money available for mortgage lending. An important part of trust company business is in the mortgage lending field-in lending . for housing purposes. The minister responsible for housing has told me the trust companies have been contacting him to stress the importance of approving these amendments if their mortgage lending is not to be curtailed, and if they are to be able to respond to the minister's request that they allocate more funds for lending for housing purposes.
At the present time, new federal trust companies may be incorporated only by special acts of Parliament and charters of existing companies can be amended only by an amending act. The amendments proposed would establish a new system of incorporating companies and amending existing charters. This would be by letters patent issued by the corporations branch of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, subject to the concurrence of the Minister of Finance. This would mean that in any application for a new charter the Superintendent of Insurance would investigate the matter just as he does now with respect to an application for a private bill. Notice of application for letters patent would be required to be published in the Canada Gazette in a way similar to that required now for the introduction of a private bill.
Existing charters, even those granted by special act of parliament, could be amended by letters patent under the proposals in the bill. Provincial companies seeking to change their status to that of federally incorporated companies would be enabled to do so pursuant to letters patent continuing the company as a federal company. However, the grant of letters patent for this latter purpose would be

December 12, 1969

subject to the concurrence of the province of incorporation and to the enactment of appropriate provincial legislation, if necessary. These changes would simplify the system of granting charters and amendments to existing charters and would permit a more effective use of the limited parliamentary time available for legislative purposes. However, the same work of inspection would be done. A standard form of letters patent would be used but there would be sufficient flexibility to provide for special circumstances; charters could contain or could be amended to impose limits on voting rights or on share ownership, if desired by the incorporators of the shareholders.
At the present time, the initial capital for any new company is specified in its private bill and is considered by Parliament on an individual basis. The proposed change in the system of incorporation also specifies that before a company may be authorized to commence business it must have a minimum capital of at least $1 million.
The proposals concerning the change in method of incorporation are similar to those proposed for insurance companies and mortgage loan companies.
A number of other amendments are also proposed. Many of these are changes in wording or changes for the purpose of altering an administrative procedure. One of the principal items dealt with is a requirement that notice of any major transfer of stock must be given to the Superintendent of Insurance at least 30 days before the transfer is to be effected, together with full information concerning beneficial ownership. This would be required in respect of the transfer of a block of stock in excess of 10 per cent of the total and in the case of a transfer which would have the effect of changing control of the company. This would not constitute a veto power in the hands of the Superintendent or of the government, but would require full disclosure and prior notice.
Another amendment would limit the maximum age of eligibility to be elected as a director to 75 years with effect from 1972. This change parallels the change which was made in the Bank Act a few years ago. Also, three-quarters of the directors of a company would be required to be Canadian citizens resident in Canada rather than only a majority as at present. This also parallels the requirement in the Bank Act.
The existing provision enabling a company to issue share warrants would be repealed.

Share warrants in this sense refer to a certificate issued by the company enabling the holder to demand certain shares of stock from the company. It is not the same as a share purchase warrant as commonly used in references to security markets at the present time. No company issues these share warrants now, and it is considered that if the practice were to be used it would be such as to defeat the provisions in the Act limiting the non-resident ownership of shares. Some amendments are proposed for the purpose of clarification with respect to the present limitations on non-resident ownership and for the purpose of specifying that voting rights of nonresidents Eire preserved if they were acquired at a time when a company was exempt from the restrictions.
Some changes are proposed in the requirements with respect to auditing. These would specify the qualifications of an auditor, to bring them into line with the specifications in the Bank Act, and the Superintendent would be given power to expand the scope of the audit if he thought this action was necessary.
A number of other less important amendments effecting, principally, changes in wording are also proposed. Hon. members will find the bill even more extensive than the amendments I have described would appear to ini-cate, particularly with respect to investment powers. This is because, under the Trust Companies Act, investment and lending powers are dealt with in three separate places. The first deals with unguaranteed trust funds, the second with guaranteed trust funds, and the third with company's own funds, that is, its capital, surplus and retained earnings.
Changes Eire proposed to transfer certain responsibilities from Treasury Board to the minister in recognition of changes in the organization of government departments.
I would be pleased to attempt to respond to detailed questions when the bill is before the finance committee. I repeat, it is considered that its approval would assist in increasing the supply of funds available for mortgage lending, particularly for housing purposes, and increase the ability of federally incorporated trust companies generally to provide services to the public. I would, therefore, ask the support of the House for this bill.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION, OPERATION AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the nature of this measure, some 58 pages in length, inspires the somewhat technical character of the statement made by the minister. This bill, dealing as it does with
December 12, 1969

restrictions on lending at arm's length, the nature of shareholdings, and so on, can be deemed to be lawyers' law. As one wanders through the bill, it takes a great deal of ingenuity to follow the particular changes that are being made.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
I would commend to hon. members for their edification the transcript of the proceedings in the other place, particularly the proceedings of Tuesday, November 18 during the presentation on second reading of the Hon. Senator John Connolly, as well as the earlier presentation on second reading by the Hon. Senator Paul Martin in May of this year.
We are dealing with a bill that has application to nine federally incorporated trust companies and ten provincially incorporated companies which are administered by the federal Superintendent of Insurance. Hon. members will note in the bill provisions to enable provincially incorporated companies to apply for incorporation under the new act by letters patent, providing there is satisfactory legislation in existence in the province in which a given trust company was originally incorporated.
As a trust company grows and wants to expand its business beyond the confines of its own province of origin, the tendency is for the company to seek federal incorporation. I think we in this House can be satisfied that the structure, examination and supervision of trust companies and insurance companies is such that the federal government system is much better than that which exists. I will not say in all provinces, but certainly in most provinces. In addition to this, as a result of the passage of the Deposit Insurance Corporation Act, it is now necessary for trust companies, certainly those that are federally incorporated, to possess a certificate of deposit insurance. Any company that would hope to do business on an openly competitive basis must have such certificate.
The minister has indicated there are many amendments to the act for the purpose of bringing trust companies in line with, or in parallel relationship with, the provisions of the Bank Act since trust companies are acting in so many ways as near banks. The other day I had occasion to complain in committee, as well as in the House, about the amendments to the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Canada Student Loans Act, which included under the term "bank" certain caisses
Trust Companies Act
populaires, trust companies, and other institutions that were carrying on some functions of banking.
I say we are approaching this question through the back door. We are gathering together a conglomerate of various financial institutions that are all related to banking or to some function of banking. I commend to hon. members the remarks I made before the banking and commerce committee at the time of the revisions to the Bank Act. I feel experience since that time has confirmed my view that we should have a general Bank Act, some of the provisions thereof dealing with the chartered banks, others with trust companies, and still others with caisses populaires. Anyone who wanted to deal with the business of banking would have to conform to the act.
If this were done we would then be able to do away with varying standards of inspection, with turning over to the Superintendent of Insurance, who is not a banker, the examination of institutions that were carrying on the functions of banking. To me, this whole matter should be brought under the one roof. I do not accept for one moment the suggestion that because trust companies and others involved in the business of banking hold a provincial charter, consent of the provinces is necessary; that the provinces have the right to sneak, through a crack in the door, into the business of banking which, under the constitution, is excusively within federal jurisdiction.
In the same way, one could say that because a small company that owned aircraft was incorporated in a province, that province would have the right to set regulations governing the operation of those aircraft. We know, of course, that this sort of thing does not happen, that no provincial government would be silly enough to try such a thing. But for some reason or other, simply because trust companies are incorporated within a province, it has been alleged that even though they are carrying on banking functions they must be supervised by the province. That is: u'ter nonsense. If such companies engage in the business of money and banking, then they must come within federal jurisdiction, which is as it should be.
I repeat that ultimately we must have a general Bank Act, a sort of omnibus act that would embrace all of the matters before us, and so that there would be no restrictions on loans by trust companies. I hope that I have made my point, but I intend to come back to it at every possible occasion. In this regard I

December 12, 1969
Trust Companies Act
commend the words of the Hon. Senator Jacques Flynn, pronounced on November 18. Speaking of the province of Quebec, he indicated that as trust companies in the province become stronger and wish to operate outside provincial borders, there will be a tendency now to apply for federal registry. Not that there is any reflection on the operations carried on within that particular province; it is merely a case of their having done good business and wanting to expand abroad, as they should. In order to do so, of course, they must come under the federal act.
As the minister has indicated, the amendments to the act fall into four main groups. First of all, there is to be an expansion in the investment powers of trust companies so as to give them more flexibility. The second group of amendments relate to those who wish to move into the banking field but will run afoul of restrictions, as a result of which we had so many non-arm's length transactions. I am sure that the Superintendent of Insurance and the Superintendent of Banking, in their respective capacities within the Deposit Insurance Corporation, have run into interlocking transactions between trust and loan companies where loans are made not necessarily to directors or officers but to major shareholders. There are also the institutions sometimes referred to as "downstream companies". I think that the provisions that will be incorporated in the act will eliminate a great deal of such abuse.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
The only thing I am concerned about here is why a substantial interest is determined to be 50 per cent more. It seems to me that in many corporate organizations a shareholding of 50 per cent, less than 50 per cent, say even 35 per cent is a substantial interest. Surely, this would be the dominant interest. Certainly, if the shareholdings are public, an individual holding 35 per cent could have a stranglehold on the company. I hope that the Superintendent of Insurance and others, including the minister, will explain to me the rationale regarding the choice of 50 per cent as the shareholding figure in determining what is a substantial interest. There may be valid reasons, but I require some very serious explanation as to why that figure was picked. I could not agree more with the general principle of restriction but I do not understand the 50 per cent figure.

The third group of amendments deals with improved supervision. These are for the better. At the moment, qui e frankly, you almost have to use a blunderbuss to control a trust company. The regulations are not flexible enough. As a matter of fact, all the damage has been done before the Superintendent of Insurance and the minister to whom he reports can take effective action for the protection of not only those who have deposit certificates but those who may have shareholdings. They, too, must be protected.
I am sure the Superintendent of Insurance, in his capacity as one interested in deposit insurance corporations, can determine whether the operating conditions, the lending portfolio and other th.ngs are satisfactory or whether the company has exceeded its borrowing powers or has sufficient assets to cover liabilities in Canada. He is in a position to know whether there has been any transgression or whether the conditions are satisfactory. He can report any unsatisfactory condition immediately to the minister. The minister may then impose a time limit within which a company must remedy the defect. He may impose conditions on the company's licence. What is still better, and this is a real sanction, he can take control of the assets to preserve them.
We have witnessed some rather tragic occurrences. After the individuals concerned became aware that interest was being evinced in the operations, they immediately noted that the assets were being withdrawn and put beyond the reach of creditors. Then, of course, there is a final sanction regard ng the windup. While some people may complain about having to report to the Government on a quarterly basis, I think this requirement is good. Banks have to make regular statements at frequent intervals. This regulation just puts trust companies on the same basis as banks. This is another reason for having a general banking statute.
We also notice an improvement in liquid reserve requirements. These companies must have 20 per cent in so-called guaranteed funds. These funds must be guaranteed as to interest. At the present time, there is not guarantee by trust companies in respect of deposit funds. They are only guaranteed as to interest. Unfortunately, the terminology in respect of guaranteed deposits is confusing. All these companies do is guarantee the interest. There is no guarantee in respect of deposits.
December 12, 1969

I should like to talk to some of the officials of trust companies about their advertisements in this regard. This morning I heard one advertisement which absolutely guaranteed deposits at 8f per cent. That is not right. All they do is guarantee ultimately to pay 8} per cent on the deposit. In any event, it is an improvement because of the changing nature of the business, and particularly since trust companies are not paying interest rates well in excess of 8 per cent. I think some offer 9 per cent on a one year certificate.
One may say that this is excessively high on a one year deposit, but the Government of Canada is prepared to pay over 8 per cent on instant money in the form of Canada savings bonds. A $100 Canada Savings Bond is the same or equivalent to a $100 bill you might carry in your wallet, yet you have the advantage of getting 8 per cent on the saving bond as long as you hold it. These facts are really beyond reasonable explanation. In any event, if the federal government is prepared to pay that kind of interest on Canada Savings Bonds we cannot expect anything less of trust companies.
Immediately following the last issue of Canada Savings Bonds, some trust companies in Toronto actually offered to pay 9.99 per cent interest on a five year certificate based on a cumulative formula. If they can pay 10 per cent for this money, at what percentage are they lending it? Remember that this is five year, medium term money. These companies certainly must lend it at something like 14 per cent or 15 per cent in order to even pay their expenses and a proper return to the shareholders.
Another good feature is the 30 day notice of transfers of shares equal to 10 per cent of the total or what is effective control of the company. We will require a little more precision as to what the Superintendent of Insurance will consider to be effective control of a company. I certainly hope this will not be equated with substantial interest, in other words, the 50 per cent.
The amendments in the fourth group relate to incorporation. These changes do not eliminate the possibility of trust companies coming to Parliament. They give trust companies the alternative of going through the registrar of companies office under letters patent but only under certain conditions. This is not a carte blanche provision. We all know that federal incorporated trust companies, instead of having capitalization of $250,000 as is now the case, will have to have $1,000,000. While this
Trust Companies Act
allows for an inflation factor, it will in effect separate the men from the boys. People who can come up with $1 million are going to be far more serious and much better organized in order to, first of all, acquire the $1 million.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
The provision in respect of directors not being eligible beyond age 75 conforms with the Bank Act. Another provision parallel to the Bank Act is that provision requiring that | of the directors shall be Canadian citizens as opposed to a bare majority. This is all to the good. We also have restrictions in respect of non-resident owned shares for an individual being 10 per cent and for a group 25 per cent. This is on the same basis as banks. There is a non-retroactive feature. I do not think you can penalize any person who now holds more than a 10 per cent interest in a trust company. Of course, anything that individual acquires hereafter will be affected by the non-voting rights provision.
The one thing I should like to see is a provision that there shall be no resurrection of dormant charters. We think this has led to a great deal of abuse in some of the provincial jurisdictions where trust companies had been organized literally on two sheets of paper back in the 1910's and 1920's. Some of them had not even operated, but the charters were there. They really should have been stricken off, but they were still there. In some cases they were bought for less than $100. In some cases some firm of solicitors held on to a charter. Then, amendments were made to bring these charters up to date and these companies were in business. It was all very nice, but no longer will this apply.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?

speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION, OPERATION AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: I am sure he did not intend it to be inferred that this had happened in respect of any federal company. I assume his reference to dormant charters being resurrected does not apply to companies under federal jurisdiction.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION, OPERATION AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
No; I am
not aware of any federal charters being picked up in that way. Certainly, of the nine federal charters now in existence, none were picked up in this way. But these amendments are to apply to the future. Certainly, they will apply to any provincial companies which desire to come under federal jurisdic-

December 12, 1969
Trust Companies Act
tion. This may be a far-reaching operation. I think perhaps if I found a dormant provincial charter and wanted to resurrect it I could work out something. If there were enabling legislation on a general basis. I would then transfer that charter to the federal field. I think the road would be open. In any event, I hope this amendment will effectively bar that type of operation.
There are other matters which could be mentioned in respect of this bill. As I said earlier, a lot of it is lawyer's law. This is what could be called a committee bill. It may be instructive to note that the representatives of the Trust Companies Association of Canada were present at the committee hearings in the other place and were satisfied with the proposed amendments, many of which incidentally impose considerable restrictions.
Others may talk about the business of allowing an increase from 15 per cent to 20 per cent at times of capitalization. But this is subject to approval by the Governor in Council under certain conditions; it is not just a matter of automatically qualifying for this increase. We will want to know the general nature of the regulations which may be passed by the Governor in Council to cover that precise condition. On the question of owning a subsidiary in or out of Canada, subject to regulation of course, I would think myself that this is quite right. If a Canadian trust company has a subsidiary abroad it must have power to invest abroad because the country of residence of the subsidiary will impose restrictions on investment. It will insist that there be investments within that jurisdiction equal to the liabilities of the trust company subsidiary within that jurisdiction. We in Canada insist upon it and therefore must expect reciprocity. In any event, there is an absolute minimum yardstick that there must be sufficient reserves within Canada, investments in Canada, to cover Canadian liabilities.
As I said, we will want to ask more questions in committee concerning the detail. I am sure we will receive this detail. I have examined the total record in the other place and, with its exceptions of some of the features I have mentioned, I personally am satisfied that the amendments to this act are a step forward. I still maintain the general caveat I entered at the very beginning, that it seems to me we must now be giving thought, when we come to the next revision of the Bank Act some years hence, to finding ways and means to bring all banking and quasi banking institutions under the one umbrella.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION, OPERATION AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my honourable and learned friend from Edmonton West has indicated he is satisfied with the amendments to this bill. I am far from satisfied. I think there is a great deal wrong with this bill. It will have to be examined very carefully in committee. The financial institutions of this country have an overwhelmingly important role to play in the economic life of this country. The complexity of the law regulating them, as well as their awesome economic power, ought to inspire urgent and critical attention. We intend to give this attention. We do not intend to be panicked by the type of statement made by the minister earlier in the debate which was a reflection of the statement made by the House leader, affectionately known as "Mac the Knife". The contempt for Parliament indicated in the statement the House leader made the other day was matched only by his economic ignorance and his heavy-handed blackmailing tactics. He is much too transparent. We cannot understand the urgency in rushing these measures through. We do not believe the reasons given form an adequate background.
In looking at this legislation we find, first of all, that there is absolutely no control over which area of the economy will get the money as a result of enlarging the lending power of the trust companies. There is absolutely no control. We do not believe, as has been stated by the minister and by the House leader before him, that this will add one single cent of mortgage money for the people who need housing in this country. I hope at some time the minister will demonstrate how he intends to do this. Ah we are being asked to do is transfer funds from the one institution to another. The pool of savings that exists in this country, whatever it may be at any given time, will not be increased one iota by changing these regulations and increasing the authority and lending power of the trust companies. Quite the contrary. The effect of the legislation may be to dry up mortgage money. I think this should be pointed out, because in this legislation we are giving more freedom to the trust companies to make investments, including commercial loans. Trust companies have not made such loans before.
What assurance exists within this legislation that these companies will not switch to commercial loans in order to make more profit than they would from mortgages. There is no guarantee in this legislation to that
December 12, 1969

effect. The making of commercial loans would be contrary to the present practices of the trust companies, and would be a completely new and lucrative field for them. The other point is that trust companies could now have subsidiaries and this would enable them to have a substantial equity in properties for which they were providing mortgage money. Apartment buildings, commercial properties and shopping centres would be involved, but not housing. Such a provision would allow trust companies to say they want a piece of the action and that if they do not get it they will not invest. This is what this legislation provides. Yet, we are told it will provide more mortgage money and therefore we, the terrible people in the opposition, must not hold up his legislation. What kind of nonsense is propagated in that statement!
Let us look at some of the other powers that would be given to the trust companies. This bill would enable them to become involved in the real estate development business in partnership with other companies. They could own real estate, thus becoming investors in their own right. They would no longer have to lend money on mortgages but the return they would get from their mortgage operations would permit them to become investors. They could even have a subsidiary to operate mutual funds. Does the minister really mean that these altruistic financial institutions, when faced with the opportunity of making more money in commercial loans and other investments, will make more money available for housing, particularly when there is no clause in this legislation which says they must do that.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
They are being given complete freedom to operate as they wish. As if that were not enough, they can now go into foreign operations and invest outside the country, which they have not been able to do freely up to now. It does not seem possible that this legislation will result in the provision of more mortgage money in Canada when trust companies will be able to make more lucrative investments in other countries. They will then say "we can make a higher rate of return in another country, so let us raise the interest rates here". It does not make any difference how useful that investment in a foreign country may be or what the priorities of the Canadian economy may be. There are profitable opportunities outside this country and that is where investments will be made and
Trust Companies Act
the money will go. This is what this legislation is designed to encourage. So, let us be fair about this. Let us not say that the opposition, by holding up this legislation-if they intend to hold it up, which we do not intend to do-is going to hurt the people who need money for mortgages.
The other issue is that if money for mortgages were made available, what assurances exist within this legislation that that money will go to the people of this country who need housing in the worst possible way? There has been no assurance in the past and there is no assurance in this legislation. If anything, this legislation almost guarantees that the situation will be worse rather than better for those in the lower income categories who need housing. There is no shortage of mortgage money for people who can afford to pay the present interest rates or who have the necessary collateral. The problem in housing in this country is that those who need it desperately are the ones who are least able to get it, and this legislation will not change this shameful situation.
We have heard these arguments before when listening to statements from the government. They are repeated over and over again like an old record that has been brought out. The government has just scratched out a few dates and perhaps changed the title, but we heard it all before when the Bank Act was being debated. They said to us, "take off the ceiling and remove the restrictions on the banks. We need competition in this country, and competition will act to further the interests of the average Canadian". Has it done so? It certainly has not. We now have the highest interest rate in Canadian history. Surely, the Bank Act changes enabled the banks to become more competitive with the trust companies and other financial institutions. Now, the trust companies say to us "take all the restrictions off us, too, so we can compete with the banks and so we can go after the same business". So, you have them competing with each other in this particular area, but that is senseless and does not help the people of this country.
The same arguments that we heard about giving the banks freedom we are now hearing about giving trust companies freedom. But whom will it help? I submit that it will not help the people of Canada but only a small group of people who seek an opportunity to make higher profits for their institutions. It will help the trust companies, of course, but is this why we are here? Are we here to help

December 12, 1969
Trust Companies Act
trust companies, banks and financial institutions, or are we here to concern ourselves with what happens to the people in this country? I suspect that the people who are not in trust companies, insurance companies or mortgage companies are in the majority, and it strikes me that in a democracy the majority has some rights. We are not here to provide special advantages to financial institutions, but essentially that is what this legislation does. We are being asked to participate in a senseless game, played by strong men in an arena called the market place, which has no more effect on the future prosperity of this country than did the struggle between gladiators in the Roman Colosseum. It is a little game, and when we are restricting it we are told that we are restricting freedom.
We must not prevent the strong men from playing this game, regardless of the consequences to the country. It is their right to play this game, regardless of what it does to the ordinary people who are not the slightest bit interested in this nonsense. If they want to play games let them do it at their own expense, not at the expense of the people of this country. In another age these gentlemen might have been called adventurers, freebooters or buccaneers. They would have sailed wi.h Drake on the Spanish Main to rob Spanish galleons. I suggest that the conflict between the banks, the trust companies and the finance companies does not contribute to the wealth of this nation any more than the conflict between Drake and the Spaniards. It did not matter whether Drake took from the Spanish galleons or the Spaniards took from Drake. This did not contribute to increasing productivity and the goods and services needed by the people. It is merely a transfer of resources from one private pocket to another, and we are being asked to be a party to this.
This debate is very important because we are being asked to take a decisive step. We are asked to give the government the power to incorporate trust companies by letters patent, so then, these matters would no longer be debated during private members' hour. I know there are many who will say that the private members' hour was a farce; that we held up these great captains of industry and we questioned them. What right had a few members to hold up these giants of our society, these people with millions of dollars of assets? But at least we had a look at their proposals, whatever the faults may have been

with the private members' hour. I am not suggesting that we go back to that method, but at least there should be someone in this Parliament who will examine what is happening to the financial institutions of the nation. Often we were effective in bringing about some necessary and useful changes, and in focussing public attention and changing public opinion regarding the conduct of many of these institutions. This will no longer be the prerogative of parliament. It is left to the discretion of the minister to authorize the formation of these companies. The minister will determine their lending powers and at one fell swoop, at the minister's discretion, they will increase by 33 per cent their ability to make loans or take in assets. The minister has a great power, and there is nothing in the previous behaviour of this government to indicate that this power will be exercised wisely or in the public interest. We need something better than that.
* (12:50 p.m.)
We are not prepared to see this legislation pass through the House without obtaining some assurances that the people of Canada will have some say in how these financial institutions are handled. There is a critical question here as to whether the future of our society is to be decided by the scramble for booty in the vain hope that while these strong men are scrambling for profits, playing a game, flying back and forth in their aeroplanes, wining and dining each other, making deals and deciding they are going to amalgamate here, close down there and turn around elsewhere, somehow or other the public is going to benefit. It is just not true. It is part of the mythology that a small percentage of our population has been able to spread in our society through its use of organizations in which it has power, the newspapers, and through the governments in which it traditionally has had friends. But the people have not benefited from these activities. Therefore we are going to propose that certain changes be made in this legislation.
The first change we propose is that Trust Companies be brought under the Bank Act. In this regard, I agree with the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), but perhaps for other reasons. It is unthinkable that they should not be under the Bank Act, as recommended by the Porter Commission. What is strange is that, while the government has accepted those recommendations of the Porter Commission which provide advantages and
December 12, 1969

benefits to the trust companies, it has not accepted the recommendations which ensure the responsiveness of these institutions to public policy and control. Mr. Speaker, you cannot take just one part of an equation. Both parts are involved.
Our other concern is to see that the Bank of Canada, on the advice of the government, will have some say in how the money collected by these institutions will be used. As inadequate as our banks are in our present society in terms of their responsiveness to public policy, at least they are far more responsive than are the other financial institutions. At present the banks have some 15 per cent of their deposit creating facilities directed by the government of Canada. This means that through public policy we are able to see that there are some funds for student loans, that there are funds for farmers and funds for businessmen. At least something is being done.
There is absolutely nothing in this proposed legislation which would indicate that the trust companies have to respond in some way. It is absolutely imperative that before this legislation is passed an amendment be made indicating quite clearly that a percentage of the funds collected by trust companies shall be allocated according to public priorities. It is intolerable that it should be otherwise.
It is particularly galling when one listens to these giants of the financial institutions coming before House of Commons committees decrying public expenditures and calling for belt tightening. The governments always have to tighten their belts. But even using their own figures, that governments at all levels account for only one-third of the gross national product, what about the other two-thirds? What about the private sector? What about priorities out there? After all, the government has established some kind of priorities.
The public does have a say in government policy to some extent. We have an opportunity of saying in this House that the money should be spent here or there. This is what debate is all about. This is why we have parties. This why we meet and talk to each other. But what happens out in the private sector? Where is the belt tightening out there? Where are the restrictions out there? Where is the sense of obligation to the nation out there? There is none, and there cannot be any unless we insist upon it. An absolute minimum condition in any legislation is that these institutions be responsive to national
Trust Companies Act
interests and national purposes, and therefore a percentage of the loans they make should be subject to public direction.
We have to go beyond that, Mr. Speaker, and make sure that Ihe spread between what financial institutions pay for money and what they charge for money is subject to some kind of regulation. We know that imposing a ceiling does not work. It could work if the government insisted on it, but it has never insisted on it. There is difficulty imposing a ceiling on what banks can pay to depositors, but we do know we can regulate, if we will, the profit margin between what they pay to depositors and what they charge borrowers.
If we did that, the depositor would benefit enormously. There is no reason why he should not be receiving as much as he is receiving now, and those who lend money may also benefit because they may be able to get their money for something less than they are obtaining it now.
We know we have to go in*o some kind of incomes policy. We know that the government's programs and attempts to control inflation have proven worthless, and that we will have to move in new direc ions. This is one of the significant areas into which we must move. Let us be very, very clear about this. No section of the economy, whether it is industry with its prices or labour with its wages, will accept restraint when the financial institutions are free to do exactly as they please, free to make as much money as they please, free to charge whatever the traffic will bear.
If we are to talk about an incomes policy and be honest about it, instead of blaming labour because it refuses to go along with phoney suggestions, we should start right here with this legislation. No part of our economy contributes more to rising costs and inflationary psychology than do the financial institutions of Canada. An incomes policy has to start at the beginning, and this is the beginning. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we see this as important legislation.
We can understand that some of the proposed minor changes, bookkeeping changes, are necessary. But we do not see this just as lawyers' law. It is far more than lawyers' law; it should be people's law. It is not just the investors or the people who borrow from trust companies, or the people who lend money to trust companies who are concerned. There is a thing called the public interest and it is that which has to be guaranteed in the legislation before us. At the

December 12, 1969
Trust Companies Act
moment there is very little in this legislation to indicate the public interest has really been considered. Sure, it can be called lawyers' law, but we are not satisfied with that. We are all involved. Mr. Speaker, may I call it one o'clock.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION, OPERATION AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to sum up the main points of our criticism. First of all, contrary to what the House Leader said, there is no panic for this legislation. The passage of this legislation will not increase the total amount of mortgage funds available for housing and, to the extent that the trust companies increase their mortgage lending, it means a decrease in some other sector of the economy. With the enlarged powers of investment being given to the trust companies, the only possible method of increasing mortgage funds would be to charge higher interest rates than now prevail. Although mortgage funds are available now, they will have to compete with investments giving higher returns, such as consumer loans, foreign investments, equity and property in industry.
The passage of the legislation as it stands now would make it even more difficult for public bodies, municipal, federal or provincial, to attract funds because they will have to compete with the enlarged investment opportunities being given to the loan companies. All public attempts will be frustrated or, if not, we will have to pay higher rates of interest to attract funds for public purposes.
There is no indication from the government, and there certainly is nothing in this legislation, to indicate that it will meet the urgent problems of our society. The public needs, as I pointed out earlier, would be frustrated rather than enhanced, as would the need for housing for low income families. This bill will not help attain these goals.
As the legislation now stands, Mr. Speaker, it is unacceptable to this party. It will be our endeavour to see that it is corrected to benefit the people of this country rather than a small group of stockholders who stand to gain enormously from its passage.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION, OPERATION AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on Bill S-8 under consideration.
This bill is like any other one vesting in financial institutions undue powers which are not likely to help us solve our problem since it is of an economic nature. The economy does not operate properly because it cannot finance itself.
Our economic problems are not tied in with loans, since, from the beginning of Confederation, Canadians have borrowed money to such an extent that they cannot pay the interest any longer and these new institutions will lend money to other institutions to enable them to pay the interest on their indebtedness. That will not solve the problem of interest rates which not only are too high but are a bare-faced exploitation of the population. Moreover, as mentioned by the hon. member from the New Democratic party, it will not add a penny to money in circulation. If there is not enough money in circulation and if reimbursements exceed credit, there can never be any money in circulation.
What we do have now is a high cost of living and tight money problem. The new institutions being established are to lend funds collected through new bond issues since even if they do not issue money as credit banks do, they will be empowered to issue bonds, which is even worse than bank issues of money. For each dollar deposit, the banks grant $96 in credit, whereas the bonds issued by the trust companies have no more value than the credit extended by the banks.
When bonds are floated, they are guaranteed by the stocks or the assets of the borrowers.
Bonds have been and are still being issued. In this connection, I will quote from an article in last December 12 issue of La Presse. In fact, here is how the article reads:
In these days of high living costs and, we might add, exorbitant spending (in spite of requests for restraint), individuals-and perhaps even more so -municipalities are liable to run excessively into debt. They have not failed to do so, particularly during the last decade or so, to wit the unhappy results published in this paper yesterday under the heading "towns of Quebec collectively on the verge of a financial dead-lock".
In order to pin down the subject without changing the author's concept, we quote the first few lines of Florian Bernard's article: "The municipalities of Quebec are going into debt at an alarming rate. Only the very wise could say whether this is a sign of progress or recession. One thing is certain: Quebecers are now virtually up to their necks in debt."
December 12, 1969

Here is a sample of eloquent statistics: "The net funded debt of Quebec's 1,652 municipalities has just reached $2,083 million at the end of this fiscal year. Since it stood at $1,886 million last year, it shot up by $102 million in only twelve months. This rate of increase in municipal indebtedness has been constant in the last ten years or so, and if the present trend continues our indebtedness will (unfortunately) top the $3 billion mark within two or three years. In only ten years, from 1957 to 1967, the total debt of the 1,652 municipalities in Quebec increased from $625 million to $2,083 million..." It has therefore tripled. Obviously the same applies to the per capita debt of the Quebecer which has climbed to $355 from $113 in eight years.
That is the debt of the Quebec municipalities alone. The debt of the school boards is three times greater. Now to settle the problem, we will allow various financial institutions to lend money at any rate they wish. They will demand interest rates of 15, 20 per cent, but it does not matter. It is alleged that this will solve the problem, but there does not seem to be any solution.
I do not object to many institutions lending money, provided there is control, however, and the interest rate does not remain unchecked.
I have here another newspaper article entitled: "More than $318 million in bonds in November". It reads as follows:
The bond issues to finance the various levels of government and the companies in Canada have reached a total of $318,390,043 last month.
Excluding the Canada savings bonds, the amount of which is not yet available for 1969, this figure compares with $131,249,864 in November 1968. The Canada savings bond sold in November 1968 amounted to $3,125,000,000.
For the first eleven months of this year, the bond issues totalled $4,399,479,079, compared to $7,898,272,174 for the same period in 1968.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
The government of Canada has not issued any bonds maturing in three years or more, in the last month. However, for the first eleven months of the year, this amounted to $1,115 million, as compared with $5,162,500 for the same period last year.
With regard to provincial governments, their direct and guaranteed financing by way of bonds has reached $188,750,000 last month, as compared with $85 million in November 1968.
The most important provincial issues have been for $50 million by the Ontario Hydro and the Quebec government; $50 million (American) by Manitoba and $35 million by Nova Scotia. Provincial loans on that market, since the beginning of the year, amount to $1,460,577,200 as compared to $1,375,700,000 from January to November 1968.
On the other hand, municipalities have borrowed in the same way $73,690,043 last month as compared with $40,149,824 in November 1968.
Bonds have therefore been issued at prohibitive rates of interest. When they are
Trust Companies Act
bought back by banks all at the same time, new deposits are created thus. Indeed, to make use of the power they have to create new credit, banks need only pen and ink. It is all it costs them.
On the other hand, people are more and more concerned. They are no longer able to get out of this stagnation. The depth of the precipice is such that there is, indeed, no hope of getting out. We cannot break surface and get over the precipice.
If we carry on in this way, what solution shall we find? How will people be able to keep paying taxes? Everything they have built is already taken away from them!
As we produce goods, we get into greater debt. There is no reason for that. All trust companies, insurance companies and exploiters of the people should be brought around. We do not advocate the socialization of institutions but we want them to be reasonable with regard to their loans. Exploiters must cease to skin the population the way they do. The responsibility does not lie in the hands of the institutions but in those of members of parliament and of the government administration. They have the power to create and increase credit. It is a sovereign right that belongs to the state. Therefore, Canada must avail itself of its sovereignty concerning the creation and issue of new credit. It should finance public funds without charging interests.
Is it still possible to continue to finance municipalities and school boards on the verge of bankruptcy which must borrow at the new excessive interest rates to pay another loan raised five or ten years ago?
If a municipality or a school board is compelled to repay bonds issued ten years ago at 5 per cent and now due, even if the collection of taxes has not been sufficient to make the repayment, it now has to raise some new loans to repay those bonds.
If those bonds were issued at 5 per cent, the interest would amount to $50,000 per million dollars. With the new rate of 8 per cent, the interest would amount to $80,000 per million dollars. If municipalities and school boards are unable to pay a 5 per cent interest, how will they manage to pay 10 or 15 per cent to the same person?
We should be striving to solve the problems instead of making them worse. What we are doing is applying a poultice to a wooden leg, and this will merely allow institutions to get rich at the expense of the taxpayers, to sink them deeper, to deprive them of their money

December 12, 1969
Trust Companies Act
and to drive them more quickly to bankruptcy. That is what is in store for us and for municipalities, school boards and private enterprises.
We would be surprised at the amount of indebtedness of private institutions. It is impossible to tolerate any longer such a system. We must say it again and again, because we are here to try to solve problems, to protect the people, to set up a sound system in order to finance our production and to prevent exploitation of the people.
The proposed improvements will only create difficulties, deprive the taxpayers even more and discourage the people who are already disheartened enough.
In fact, people do not even want to work any longer, or have to work for the government.
When plant workers are asked to work overtime, they refuse, because the additional income they thus make is whittled away by income tax. The result is that production dwindles instead of rising.
Hon. members should consider more carefully these corporate structures with a view to making them institutions that will serve the government, of which we all are shareholders. The government makes profits, which are distributed among a few individuals, while others are overtaxed, and as production increases, the holdings of Canada, of financial ins itutions and of individuals also increase.
Those holdings are transferred to the assets of financial institutions and all the bodies who built the country are entered as liabilities, and they are hopelessly sunk.
In conclusion, I should like to point out that the hon. member of the New Democratic party is right but only in a proportion of 60 per cent, because we do not want to socialize everything as he does. We, of the Ralliement creditiste, wish to keep private enterprises as healthy as possible. However, we do not want those institutions to exploit but rather to serve people.
Credit should be a state-controlled affair. Instead of having different institutions issuing bonds to municipalities, the government, through its own bank, should issue such credit, at a depreciation rate of 5 per cent and perhaps 1 per cent for administration costs, which would bring the interest rate to 6 per cent instead of 10, 15 or 20 per cent, and would allow municipalities, school boards, private institutions, manufacturers and all those in need of capital to get themselves out of a hole.

Private institutions, as well as banks, trust companies and insurance companies, should manage to lend only the capital in circulation. They would not be allowed to isssue bonds, to grant credits or make capital available.
All we want is to socialize the creation of credit, but the allocation of credit by financial institutions could be carried out in the manner used by credit unions.
To play with credit, to make loans at one's own discretion to both private and public institu ions would come under the state's responsibility, for it alone is in a position to finance our public institutions. Thus we would ensure a greater purchasing power for the taxpayers, since public institutions would stop depriving private institutions of their assets. In fact, they are robbed of their right to live, to act, to produce and to expand.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION, OPERATION AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, most of the amendments suggested to the Trust Companies Act appear to be designed to strengthen those corporations and provide additional protection to investors and the public. I can see little to criticize in their intent, except perhaps that they do not go far enough.
My chief concern is with clauses which it is claimed will set more funds flowing into the mortgage market and thus stimulate home building. Again, this is a worthy objective, but the proposal may well be only an empty gesture. Similar amendments proposed to the Trust Companies Act and the Loan Companies Act fall in the same category. It is obvious that the reason the government is rushing in now with these amendments is that it has given up any hope of controlling run-away interest rates and is unable to fulfil its bold promise of dramatic advances in home building.
These amendments to the various insurance, trust and loan company acts are an inadequate answer to the Canadian housing crisis. They constitute a confession of failure on the part of the government to fulfil its promises and to find a sound, long-range policy for providing the number of housing units needed annually by our expanding society.
I believe the government has acted in panic and has been stampeded into grasping at the first straw in sight. A little forethought, a little foresight, would surely have shown that just because legislation is brought in permitting the various types of loan companies to expand their investments in mortgages, these
December 12, 1969

companies will not necessarily leap into the mortgage market with vast sums in new investment dollars. It is a case of leading a horse to water and finding oneself unable to make it drink. If insurance companies can make better, more lucrative and shorter term investments than mortgages from their small pool of investment money, they will make them where it is most profitable, government permission or not.
The fact that an act of Parliament permits trust companies to invest in mortgages on an extended basis is no guarantee that they will do so. Apparently the government hopes that these amendments will increase the funds available to the residential building field. I believe it is quite likely that what extra mortgage investment is permitted by the amended Act will go into commercial and industrial building.
It is interesting to look back at the record of the insurance companies in the mortgage investment field. According to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation figures for the month of July last, a total of $110 million was advanced in mortgages under the National Housing Act. Of this, CMHC itself provided $36 million, trust and loan companies $32 million, chartered banks $25 million and insurance companies $17 million. The figures indicate that this is the proportion which has prevailed over the past five years at least.
It appears clear that while the government continues to pursue restrictive and unselective monetary policies, the necessary flow of mortgage money to feed our starving home building program will not be forthcoming. The mere provision of permission to invest more widely will not guarantee that investment will take place.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
Most insurance, trust and loan companies are in a real bind with regard to liquidity today. Funds are scarce, and they are not likely to be placed in a market where they will earn less and be tied up longer than in many other available investment areas.
I think the minister has done a grave injustice to this question of providing housing by producing this meagre answer to a problem that goes far beyond the social implications of providing housing. It is inextricably bound up with the whole socio-economic problem of urban living, a problem which this government has so far successfully kept at arm's length.
Trust Companies Act
As reported in the Globe and Mail for December 4, Herbert Hignett, president of CMHC, said:
More money has been spent on housing per capita in metropolitan Toronto in recent years than anywhere in North America but the public has received less for its money in terms of housing for all citizens.
Mr. Hignett attacked the philosophy of some builders that homes for people of modest incomes cannot be produced. He said that the number of housing units built meant very little indeed if only one person in six could afford the houses, and one in three the apartments. Mr. Hignett's remarks indicate to me something of the great complexity and menacing social overtones of Canada's particular housing problem. We must not only find mortgage funds in times of oppressively heavy interest rates and extreme investment competition, but must make those funds produce houses where, when and of a type that is needed.
We must look at housing as a problem with dimensions other than simply financial. The Winnipeg Free Press of November 27, at the conclusion of an editorial commenting on the recent presidential commission report in the United States on crime and violence, had this to say:
There was a moment in our experience when Paul Hellyer seemed to be saying things about housing and smaller towns that had meaning in terms of social health.
Is there now anybody in government who thinks of housing as anything but more impersonal sardine cans where more people can feel unrelated to more people?
If, as I and many other Canadians believe, housing is indeed a problem of national social health, then such feeble pinprick attempts to tackle the question as are represented by these amendments are totally inadequate. I wonder if the government has given any consideration to the methods employed by several advanced European countries to meet a similar housing problem. I believe it would be beneficial if the government were to look at the way building societies operate in Great Britain, where the principle of thrift, pooled resources and co-operative effort are employed so satisfactorily.
On November 6 the House committee on finance, trade and economic affairs heard an expert in the field from Germany, Dr. Horst Seidler, director of the Berlin Institute of Economic Research. He explained the German system whereby housing funds were provided by savings in special building banks.

December 12, 1969
Trust Companies Act
Interest on the funds was fixed and divorced during the period of saving from the actual conditions of the capital market outside. He explained it as a method free from the need for subsidization because "it is a simultaneous process of saving by one part of the population and the giving of credit to another part of the population".
As an example, a German worker would save from 10,000 to 15,000 marks. When he wished to acquire his own home, he would borrow from the building savings bank an additional 50,000 marks at 5J per cent interest on a first mortgage. With the country's prime rate at about 7J per cent, 5J per cent appears ludicrous on the surface. The fact is that the bank can lend him the money at 5J per cent regardless of the outside rate, because it is money being saved for building purposes in a special fund and earning interest at below 5J per cent. In other words, it is a separate little financial world designed only for the provision of one special service-adequate funds at reasonable rates for home building.
These are the types of methods that I believe we should at least explore for possible adaptation to Canadian conditions. We must, I believe, make a special attack on a very special problem if we are to get anywhere. Such pitiful expedients as giving loan companies permission to invest more money in housing will never meet the need.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I will be the only member who has noted the fact that a great coincidence occurred with the introduction today of this legislation. Yesterday there was published the report of a special royal commission on the affairs of Atlantic Acceptance Corporation. Among other things, the report of that commission, which dealt with corporations under the jurisdiction of the province of Ontario, indicated that part of the source of the problem was failure on the part of the supervisory authorities to exercise control over that particular financial institution.
One thing that we in Ottawa, and in the federal government, can be proud of is the undoubted excellence of the control over financial institutions that is exercised by the Superintendent of Insurance. This control is such that it is not only a matter of particular knowledge to the members of this House, but is regarded by the financial community of Canada as being almost without peer. The office of the Superintendent of Insurance is carried on by a very small staff. The integrity

of the officials is something of which we may all be proud. The excellence of the job they have done is illustrated by the fact that none of the federal institutions under their control have ever defaulted or caused any kind of concern to the public with whom they deal.
One of the most important provisions in this legislation extends to some extent the already great powers of the Superintendent of Insurance in controlling, supervising and regulating trust companies and other companies that are being dealt with in parallel legislation. In confiding these powers to this excellent office we in this House can have confidence that they will be well used and that the public interest will be protected.
I think there is general agreement that it is very much in the public interest to make the amendments that are suggested, which have the effect of loosening and broadening the powers of trust companies. They will be able to borrow more money from the public, and fewer restrictions of a formal kind will be placed upon them in the matter of making loans to mortgagors and others.
This is not, as my hon. friend from Edmonton West suggested, merely a lawyer's bill. This is a bill of great significance to the people of Canada in that it deals with all types of corporations that touch the lives of people at many points. Trust companies deal with estate matters, with savings, with their own investments and with prospective homeowners who come to them for mortgage money. Any legislation dealing with trust companies and similar corporations is of great significance and should be carefully scrutinized.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
I hope that when this legislation is considered by the finance committee, it will be given rather more scholarly treatment than was the case in the speech of the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman), who we are told is the financial critic of his party. I think when the proposals are made, as he suggests they might be made, for amendments to the legislation it would be helpful if they were based upon an accurate assessment of what the legislation contains.

One question which clearly arose, and I would be very happy to hear the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) speak about it, is contained in the statement of the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) that it is the function of this Parliament or this government to confiscate the savings of the people. After hearing some of the statements we have listened to today, one might gather that this is an illegitimate purpose; that there is something wrong with the people of the country saving money and earning a return on it by making it available through this very convenient type of corporation for productive and social uses. I hope I misunderstood what was said by the hon. member for Dauphin.
