The available statistics show that no group of companies has made anything like the same contribution to the housing industry as have the trust companies and loan companies. Therefore, I suggest to hon. members that one very positive contribution we can make toward the alleviation of some of our housing problems in this country is to make the methods and operations of trust companies easier, giving
Trust Companies Act
them greater access to funds, and enabling them to enter even more vigorously than they have to date into the mortgage business.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION, OPERATION AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity of taking part in this debate today. I believe it is necessary that I show an interest in housing in view of the fact my leader has recently appointed me as the housing critic of this party. I must say I have a lot to learn and I think the government is in the same boat. Let me tell the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair), who is now looking through the curtains on the other side of the Chamber, that I appreciate the fact all Parliamentarians should be concerned in controlling these huge corporate structures. We all read recently about the fiasco of the Atlantic Acceptance Corporation.
My complaint relates to the fact that when the government House leader was speaking about a week ago, and correct me if I am wrong, he did not indicate he was bringing Bills S-8 and S-9 before the House in order to protect the public. He indicated rather that he was in a hurry to see these bills considered by the House and referred to a committee in order to assure greater funds in the mortgage field. Members of this party are concerned because of what he said, as illustrated by the remarks of the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie).
At this time we should question whether in fact this bill will have the results indicated by the government House leader. We must question that because there is no guarantee of this result in the bill and the government House leader had no right to make that statement. He can express his hopes and his belief that these corporate structures are responsible and therefore will continue to be in a position to help the mortgage market. In this way, the vast majority of Canadians might see some ray of hope in terms of housing.
I am also concerned because this bill will mean that these companies will have an opportunity to look to foreign fields. I should like to know the reason for this sudden interest in foreign fields. Is the market in Canada not worthwhile? Am I to understand that in order for these companies to be structured in a way that is conducive to the ultimate outcome of profits and benefits for Canadian people they have to look outside the Canadian market? This is what concerns me and what concerns other members of this party.
The Economic Council of Canada has indicated that we must continue to increase

December 12. 1969
Trust Companies Act
our stock of housing in order to reach our 1975 goal, which I understand is one million units. We cannot have a recurrence of what took place in 1966 when the number of housing units available was low. The greatest impediment toward the development of sufficient housing is the lack of mortgage money. The government should be concentrating its efforts in order to see that we do have more mortgage money rather than on this band-aid type of philosophy it has brought before us this afternoon.
We all know that lending institutions, banks, insurance companies and trust companies account for the great bulk of mortgage money. There is, of course, the residual lenders and the Government. What seems to bother Canadians throughout this land is that the volume of available mortgage money has been spotty and inadequate. The Government, in its wisdom, has seen fit to believe that CMHC is the organization which can either relieve unemployment or control the economy by placing money into the housing market at will. This is not what the Canadian people want. This has led us to believe that there is no adequate base of funds, and because there has been no adequate base there has been discouragement in terms of employment. Of course we are very concerned about this and the fact that the Government has not realized it should adopt a policy to guarantee a continual flow of funds from CMHC in order to assist the housing market.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Because of this uncertainty in respect of mortgage moneys it has been said that housing production is only 75 per cent of what it should be. In other words, we are not putting forth our best effort. The other day I was fortunate to receive a document from Mr. William M. McCance, Director of Research, National House Builders Association. I should like to quote some of his statements which I think are important and really to the point. He says:
There is a definite need to make increased amounts of money available on a continuing basis for all forms of shelter, as well as all income classes, to meet the estimated needs, which lie ahead. This can only be accomplished by broadening the supply of mortgage financing and in examining entirely new concepts in the method of raising housing money.
Private enterprise, for instance, is prepared and anxious to produce housing under the limited dividend provisions of the National Housing Act but Federal funds are presently unavailable for this type of financing. This is unfortunate since

it would be possible to produce a large volume of units for the lower to middle income group under these provisions.
Several provinces have enacted condominium legislation which permits the sale of individual units in a multiple housing building. Builders, however, have found it virtually impossible to interest the lending institutions in this form of investment. The condominium concept could result in individual home ownership at prices substantially below the present cost of single family houses.
Many lenders, likewise have begun to show a decided preference for large single loans on multifamily developments since there is less administration involved and they are often able to participate in part of the equity as well. These large loans have deprived the single family house builder of mortgage funds, which he formerly found available to him.
This is what we must be concerned about. Will these trust companies just become involved in putting out large sums of money or will they really become concerned about the average person who still has the old dream of owning his home? My friend from Waterloo indicated he has a fear that mortgage funds may dry up as a result of this legislation. I do not know whether they will dry up. I have some concern about whether these companies will concentrate on overseas investment. I think, however, their record is not bad. If I may refer to the appendix to the sixty-fifth report of the committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, we find that in 1964 the trust companies, in the first six months, invested $399 million in new residential, $190 million in existing residential and $94 million in other. We see that in 1968, the trust companies invested in new residential $528 million, in existing residential $257 million and in other $114 million. So, we have statistics which indicate that the trust companies are involved in mortgages. There can be no doubt about this.
What we are concerned about today is whether the trust companies will put more money into mortgages rather than move into the foreign investment field. We must be concerned about what they do in terms of the inequitable geographical distribution of mortgage money in our nation. We must be concerned about whether they place their moneys in the city of Toronto or the city of Montreal and forget about the areas on the east coast which are faced with regional disparity or the areas on the west coast. I do not see anything in this bill to give us any hope in this regard.
There is another area with which I believe this government must be concerned in respect of housing. I refer to the high interest rates.
December 12, 1969

High interest rates are killing the old Canadian dream of home ownership and are slowly turning this country into a country of landlords and tenants. I think we must be concerned about this. It is difficult to understand how anyone in this country can own a home until this government realizes that, even though the people desire to own homes, they simply cannot do so with these rates of interest.
The interest rate in respect of approved lenders in 1968 was 8J per cent and now it is up to 10 per cent. The rate for apartments and townhouses in 1968 was 8| per cent, and now is up to 94 per cent and 10J per cent. In respect of conventional presold and resale housing, in 1968 the interest rate was 9 per cent and 94- per cent. Now, it is up to 10 per cent and 10J per cent. This government must be concerned because it said we will reach our objective of one million units. I say the figure of one million units cannot be reached until sufficient money is available at rates of interest which are attractive to those who wish to become involved in owning their own home.
The other day I believe all of us received a letter from the Mortgage Insurance Company of Canada under date of December 5, 1969, in which we find the following:
November brought no brightening of the mortgage picture across Canada. Mortgage funds continued in extremely short supply, and interest rates increased slightly in some areas.
Then, we see the following:
Several reporters mention "buyer resistance to high prices and high interest rates". Another observation made in the same vein was that the desire for home ownership is as strong as ever, but that would-be purchasers simply cannot afford the high prices and the high cost of financing.
That certainly must speak for itself.
Why can we not approach the mortgage problem by way of pension funds? I understand that these funds represent a great source of untapped money, some $8 billion. At the present time I believe something in the order of 11 per cent of this money is involved in housing. I think perhaps we should convince the trustees and administrators of this vast fund of money that housing is an area in which there is continual appreciation because of inflation and what not, whereas in everything else there is depreciation. I think we should pursue that area in order to be in a position to say we are attacking this problem with some gusto.
I should like to mention another area which I think is of some significance. I have asked
Trust Companies Act
questions about this. Rather than bring in this bill-I do not know what to call it; it is not what one could term legislation of great impact in respect of housing, but maybe it is control-why could we not become involved with building societies. Is this an evil phrase? There is another irritating point with respect to housing. Ontario has asked the federal government to say exactly how much money it will loan the province for housing in 1970 to avoid the federal delays which hampered the provincial building program last year. Trade Minister Stanley Randall said Wednesday...

I think there are some fairly profound implications in what the government is now proposing. I think it is clear that it is opting for the status quo, for what we know is inadequate. The government is hoping that by tinkering with the mechanics of the legislation by way of some specific items and provisions contained in the bill, it can quieten down the public and avert the storm of protest that would probably arise if it did not take any action at all.

speechtext:
I think it ill behooved the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) to suggest that he wanted to hear a rather more scholarly dissertation from the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman). I think that the people of Canada and this House owe the hon. member for Waterloo a debt of gratitude because he put some of the fundamental issues before the House today.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton was quite erroneous in his interpretation of some of the remarks of the hon. member for Waterloo. The latter did not state that this legislation would allow trust companies to enter the personal loan field or the real estate field without any limits. I think the implication left by the hon. member for Waterloo was that trust companies could enter these fields to the extent that their policy determined, and this bill will give them all the authorization they are seeking. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton said he hoped that this sort of defective scholarly approach would not be present when the bill is before the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. I hope that when the bill is before the committee some of the fundamental considerations which need to be taken into account will be raised and discussed.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton suggested that trust companies are a very convenient type of corporation for making loans available for housing and other worth while purposes. He went on to argue that more money is needed for housing. However, in the very next sentence he suggested that the trust and loan companies have done more
Decembei 12, 1969

than anyone else in the way ol financing housing. This may very well be the case. However, there is a contradiction between these two statements because it is evident, by the admission of the hon. member, that what has been done up till now has been inadequate. I suggest that the situation in the future will not be helped materially by the provisions of this legislation, and certainly the social capital required in Canada will not be provided automatically by making it easier for trust companies to operate.
It seems to me that there are two basic considerations before the House. One-and this area was dealt with by the minister-has to do with the operations of the companies. This involves the shareholders' and the depositors' interest. There is a legitimate place for the consideration of these interests within the framework of operations of these companies as authorized in legislation passed by the Parliament of Canada. This involves, quite properly, consideration of the internal aspect of the operations; it involves various housekeeping considerations. There are in the bill a number of such considerations. It also involves problems of safeguards for the shareholders, for depositors, for purchasers of debentures, for all those who deal with these companies. These safeguards are necessary because these companies are dealing with the public.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
As was noted by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair), certain problems which originated in the past several years have occupied the attention of many people in Canada. But it seems to me there is a wider interest. There must be concern for the public interest if we are to examine the full scope and implications of this bill. It seems to me there is not in this bill an adequate consideration of the public interest.
When we deal with the role of trust companies and other companies that we will be considering in later bills, we deal with matters such as the role of finance in the economy, the role that is to be played through finance companies, how they are to affect the performance of the economy and their impact on the economy. It goes beyond that, because it has a critically important effect on the lives of people in Canada. It has an effect on the welfare and well-being of people throughout Canada, and many people far from the immediate reach of these companies are affected by the decisions they make in carrying on their day-to-day operations. In the face 21545-51
Trust Companies Act
of this situation, what is the government's attitude? It seems to be: Let them do it. Let them go ahead and do their thing and we will see there are some controls to protect the shareholders' interests, and safeguards so that they do not get into trouble which will make us the subject of public criticism.
It is obvious to all of us in this House, and to people throughout Canada, that difficulties have been encountered by the government in dealing with the current economic situation. The fact is that the fiscal and monetary restraints introduced by the government have not been effective. They have had no real effect in dealing with the inflation psychology which has been of great concern to the government. The fact is that the private sector of the economy has continued on its way without any feeling of restriction; it has carried out its activities unimpeded by the controls about which the government made a great fuss when introducing them. There has been no real restriction or restraint on the role played by the private sector of the economy in the present situation, about which the government professes to be greatly concerned. The fact is that decisions affecting the public interest are often, because of the structure of our economy, made by those controlling financial sources.
We have to ask: Where is real economic power held in Canada? It must be acknowledged by all that a great deal of the economic power in Canada is held in the private sector, and that that power is not widely diffused in the old classical sense. The fact is that a good deal of that power is concentrated in so few hands that those hands are able to deal very closely with the government. They are able to deal with it very much on an equal basis, so that the government, which speaks for the people of this country, is not able to play as effective a role as it might in dealing with the economic problems that must be faced.
We must take into account the realities of the world. Canada and the world have changed. No longer have we a situation in which power is widely diffused, in which we have a large number of small operations in all sectors of the economy. We do not have a widely diffused economic structure in this country any more. A large part of the economic power is in the hands of a relatively small number of corporations, many of which operate beyond national borders. In fact it has been suggested by people close to the situation, such as George Ball, Under Secretary of State in the U.S. government of President Johnson, that the power of the future will be

in which interest rates have been allowed to skyrocket over the last couple of years. I suggest that the Canadian public is not willing to put up with this situation indefinitely. Government policy as it has been developed until now will not be effective in controlling interest rates in Canada. Our whole economic structure is becoming increasingly fragile on the basis of the policies being followed by this government.
When introducing this bill the minister said that there is need to increase the supply of funds for housing. The hon. member for Waterloo has already dealt with this point and I referred to it earlier. Private financial institutions have had every opportunity to show that adequate funds were available to the Canadian public for housing and to see that these funds were made available on a reasonable basis, allowing people on moderate incomes to proceed with their plans to construct decent homes. I suggest that on the basis of the legislation before us there will be no further progress in dealing with the housing problem of this country; that is, essentially, the problem of housing for people of low and moderate incomes. I suggest that no more progress will be made in the future than has been made over the past several years.
There are in the bill a number of proposals which would widen the power of trust companies. I suppose it might be said that this will better enable these companies to serve the public. I suggest that it will be a case of gouging the public. I think this reflects the government's attitude which is inadequate and is causing an increasing degree of frustration and resentment throughout Canada.
It is also interesting to note the attitude of some of the finance companies as exhibited in recent weeks. Over the past two or three months a number of financial institutions have made representations to the Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs Committee on the subject of interest rates. Each had an explanation with respect to the current difficulties and for the record established in rising interest rates. On one thing all were unanimous-each said, no more controls. Mr. Speaker, when these companies make this type of assertion, I become suspicious. That is what they are afraid of, because they know it would put an end to the policies they have been following over the past few years. They seem to be afraid of public action. Why? Are they afraid that their vested interests will be hurt in some way?
Trust Companies Act
No proposals have been made that they should not receive a just return on their investment. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton referred to this concept. I do not know whether he feels that safeguards to protect the public from high interest rates or rates which must be defined as usury will harm the trust and loan companies. On the basis of our economic structure and the freedom of action granted to them in this bill, I suggest they are unwilling to accept their share of responsibility in the development of our country.
I further suggest that the government has been blind to the direction in which it is leading the economy. It has exhibited a blind acceptance of the status quo. There has been no discussion or consideration of the public interest. That is totally lacking in this bill and in its presentation by the government. There seems to be an attitude of see nothing, hear nothing and do nothing that will in any way harm the government's friends in the financial world who are making a very good living out of the distress in which many Canadians find themselves. On that basis, Mr. Speaker, I cannot support the bill as it is now before the House.

One is general enough to include the next bill that we will be considering, and since I think many members, like myself, would like to get out of here by Christmas, 1971, if not Christmas 1969 or 1970, perhaps I might be permitted to refer to both points at the same time.
Before I make the two points, I should like to compliment the minister who has responsibility for this bill. I think he made an

excellent categorization of the points contained in the measure, but I do not think there was an adequate explanation of the philosophy behind the two bills in respect of trust and loan companies. However, in an illustrative way he did go over half the course.

They are afraid that the power of trust and loan companies to invest in municipal securities of the country may be reduced as a result of provisions contained in clause 24 of this and the next bill. Without further ado and because I am confident that people will be good enough to raise the question in committee, I will just put the resolution on the record and trust my colleagues on that committee to study the matter and ask the necessary questions.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I would like to be in the committee to ask these questions, but we all belong to different committees. Even if one had the agility of a flea and the ability of Superman to pierce through the walls around this building, he still could not attend all the committees which meet at various times and deal with various topics. The resolution that was passed by the Municipality of the County of Halifax earlier this year reads as follows:
That whereas Bill No. S-38-

-which is a bill of the Senate of Canada, and presumably will go to the House of Commons some time this Fall, has been brought to the attention of

That whereas Bill No. S-38 will make it imperative that Federal loan companies carry in their investment portfolio cash on Federal and Provincial Government bonds for liquidity purposes and .iunior government bonds will not be acceptable for such purposes unless they are guaranteed by the appropriate Provincial Government:

The committee that studies this measure and the next one should have a clear opinion as to whether the municipalities of

It is provided that there be a policy of mortgage insurance issued by an insurance company registered under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act or the Foreign Insurance Companies Act. The point I raise is that on its face the provision perhaps represents a very valid step forward in trying to provide more mortgage financing, especially in these times of high cost, for the building of homes. From my experience when dealing with traditional lending companies and with whatever high risks one thinks are inherent in an inflationary situation, you get into a situation that is a little beyond that contemplated in the pious words of this part of the bill.
Most hon. members who are lawyers have dealt with mortgage financing. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill S-8 is very important and complex. It is one of a group of bills that deals with financial matters and originated in the other place. When I read the debates of the other place and the evidence given before the banking committee, I thought it fell short of the scrutiny that the bill deserved.
It is fair to say that when this bill was first introduced in May in the other place it took no more than half an hour to deal with it, and there were only two speakers. It is difficult to determine any difference between the two speeches, the one which was supposed to present the government's position and the other the position of the opposition. The bill had a very short stay in the banking committee. The main witness was the Superintendent of Insurance, Mr. Humphry. He seemed to be the main spokesman with regard to these bills. He enlightens the senators with regard to the provisions of this bill. One would think that in the other place, where there is so much corporate experience among the Senators, they would have been anxious to use their experience and knowledge when dealing with this important bill.
This bill was again dealt with in November and we had the same situation. There were again, two speakers and it is difficult to determine any difference in philosophy regarding this bill. Again it was rushed through the banking committee and was then presented for third reading. Perhaps so many members of the other place have such a wide financial interest in so many financial institutions that they felt they were ruled out of order because of a conflict of interest. If this was the case, it underlines the necessity for bringing forth legislation requiring Senators to declare their assets when they are appointed to the other place. If cabinet ministers have to divest themselves of their interests, surely Senators should at least declare their assets, the companies in which they are involved, the directorships they hold and the number of shares they have in these companies, so they can direct their attention to these very important bills.
We in the New Democratic Party have said there are many shortcomings in Bill S-8. We will also say there are many shortcomings in other financial bills. We cannot support the

December 12, 1969
Trust Companies Act
bill as it has been presented to the House today. The reason we do not support it encompasses five main grounds, and I would like to state those grounds, Mr. Speaker.
1.	The government of Canada should bring all financial institutions under the jurisdiction of the Bank of Canada.
2.	The Bank of Canada should regulate the loan ratios of all financial institutions.
3.	The public interest of all Canadians should be protected by a nominee of the Bank of Canada on each board of the different financial institutions.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
4.	The Government of Canada should set out a list of priorities for the public benefit and interest, and these priorities should be incorporated into the lending policies of the financial institutions.
5.	The Bank of Canada should be given the power to regulate the rate of financial return to those financial institutions.
Let me deal with the first proposition. It is saying no more than was recommended by the Porter Commission on Banking which pointed out that trust companies are very much like banks; in fact, the Commission referred to them as near-banks and said it was necessary that they should come under the jurisdiction of the federal government. One would think that the financial institutions of a country should be efficient and responsive to the needs and priorities of Canadians, yet when I look at the activities of the Bank of Canada I find it has not been a leader in this direction. I find that the Bank of Canada is the apologist for the chartered banks as well as being an apologist for the inaction of the government in dealing with the financial problems we are experiencing.
It would be fair to say we have a proliferation of financial institutions, some of them being trust companies. Evidence shows that there are nine federally incorporated trust companies administered by the federal authority, and ten provincial trust companies administered by the federal Superintendent of Insurance. This means there are 19 trust companies under federal jurisdiction. In addition, there are between 45 and 47 provincially incorporated trust companies which operate entirely within the confines of the province which incorporated them. Therefore, we find roughly one-third of the trust companies under federal jurisdiction and two-thirds under provincial jurisdiction.

It might be worth noting that the federal trust companies have $3.5 billion in assets to administer and that the provincial companies have about $10.8 billion. This is no small amount of money; the size of these assets is one of the main reasons we think trust companies should fall within federal jurisdiction and come directly under the guidance, control and regulation of the Bank of Canada. I do not know how many loan companies there are, but we find there are 65 trust companies operating across Canada, and in these circumstances one can appreciate the difficulty of obtaining efficiency and getting a response to the social needs of the country.
With regard to the proposition that the Bank of Canada should regulate the loan ratios of all financial institutions, it has been pointed out that the trust companies began with an investment authority amounting to ten times the ratio of their capital and surplus. The ratio was increased to 15 times, and now the trust companies are asking that it be raised to 20 times the amount of their capital and surplus. The minister has told us that the purpose of increasing the ratio is to make more money available for housing, but it has been ably argued by members of my party that this increase in no way supplies new money; all it does is reallocate the savings of Canadians which flow into the financial institutions.
We have said there should be direction of the investment portfolios of trust companies so that they would take care of the housing needs of Canadians. In considering the increased investment powers of these companies one has the right to be very dubious with regard to the extent to which an increase in the money available for housing will result from an increase in the permitted loan ratio. In all likelihood we will find that there is actually a decrease in the amount provided for housing. For my part, I have seen no evidence of any great interest by the trust companies in the housing needs of Canada, more especially with regard to public housing and housing for low-income groups. They were finally persuaded, after a good deal of urging, to invest in condominium housing but their record to date has not been a very proud one in this field. We say, therefore, that provision should be made for a definite percentage of the investment portfolio of these companies to be directed into housing.
I now turn to the proposition that the public interest of all Canadians should be protected by placing a nominee of the Bank of
December 12, 1969

Canada on each board of these financial institutions. Mr. Speaker, it is difficult to determine who are the true owners of the financial institutions in Canada today. They operate what is known as a cosy club; it is difficult to break through the chain of ownership which prevails. I recall that when we were studying the Bank Act in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs we suggested there should be a representative of the consumers of Canada on the board of directors of all the banks. This was refused. We also suggested that since the trade unions deposited large sums in the banks for purposes of saving, and so forth, there should be a representative from the trade unions sitting on the board of directors of the chartered banks. Again, this proposal was ignored. We are now saying that to protect the public interest, there should be a nominee of the Bank of Canada sitting on the boards of all the financial institutions of the country. No act should be slanted in such a way as to protect the privileged few in our society; all acts should be slanted toward the protection of the majority.
We recommend that there be a list of all those who hold substantial shares in our financial institutions-a list which would be accessible to the public. I cannot help wondering who does, in fact, own the majority of the shares in some of these banks, trust companies and loan companies. The fancy corporate techniques which are used today tend to cover up the true facts about ownership. One finds it difficult to strike at the true owners when such practices prevail.
My fourth point is that the government should set out a list of priorities for the public benefit and that these priorities should be incorporated in the policies of the lending institutions. At present we find the chartered banks operating under the suasion of the government. It has been said that 15 per cent of all their loans has been directed to such fields as housing, student loans, small business loans, and so on. This should not be achieved through suasion, Mr. Speaker; it should be done through direction. We should direct that a percentage of their loans be made available, without delay, for public purposes.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I recall the experience of 1968 when at the beginning of the fall the minister in charge of housing, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), realized there would be a shortage of housing in Canada. What did he do at that time? He directed moneys that had been
Trust Companies Act
earmarked for the public sector to the private sector for housing purposes. In other words, a shortfall in housing had been created by a shortage of housing money provided by banks and trust companies, and the minister had to sacrifice money that was earmarked for public housing by diverting it into the field of private housing.
It is fair to say that trust companies, like other companies today, are lending at very high rates of interest. When I see advertisements used by trust companies as gimmicks to attract customers and saving accounts, I am sick to my stomach. Big cards are displayed offering household items free if you become a customer. Other placards offer loans at 8 per cent interest. No wonder Canadians are finding it difficult to meet their financial needs.
I recall an occasion when the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) introduced a bill on behalf of the Huron and Erie Trust Company. During the debate in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) asked one of the directors of the company what would be a fair return on the money they obtained. This gentleman suggested that a fair return would be between 1 and 2 per cent. A reasonable profit of between 1 and 2 per cent could be obtained by these companies, yet they are paying 8 per cent interest to depositors and charging mortgagors and other borrowers 10 to 12 per cent interest. I think that interest rates have reached an extortionate level, and it is time the government stepped in and took immediate action.
My fifth point is that the Bank of Canada should be given power to regulate the rate of return of financial institutions. In the last few weeks financial returns of banks have indicated that their profits are enormous. The same can be said about trust companies. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) hopes that the market mechanism in regard to interest rates will come into operation. Surely he has discovered by this time that the market mechanism for adjusting interest rates is outmoded, that we should at least try a floating rate of exchange of the kind which has been so successful in other countries, and at the moment particularly in Germany. It has been said that money is the root of all evil, but surely it is the love of money that is the root of all evil. Certainly the practices of trust companies and other financial institutions whose sole determination is to make

December 12, 1969
Trust Companies Act
money have created a great deal of evil within our society.
If I may turn my attention to the bill itself, I find broad changes are being made to the act to permit trust companies to incorporate by letters patent instead of by way of special Act of Parliament; to allow companies which have been incorporated by special Act of Parliament to amend their charters without passing another special Act of Parliament. I imagine that these amendments are the result of tenacious efforts by members of my party to expose the practices of some financial institutions. The members of the New Democratic Party have attempted to slow up the progress of certain bills because of the inherent dangers in them to the public of Canada. For this we make no apology. In fact, we are quite proud of our achievement as a party in putting before Canadians some of the inherent dangers that lie in the practices of trust companies and other financial institutions.
The bill enables provincially incorporated trust companies, when authorized by provincial law, to continue as federally incorporated companies without the requirement of passing a special act in each case. The bill gives power to trust companies to widen their scope of investment, more especially with regard to foreign companies. The bill also prohibits investment where transactions are not at arm's length; and there are other amendments in regard to investment similar to those relating to insurance companies.
Some of these administrative changes are welcome; others are in need of close scrutiny. When I read the debate in the Senate on introduction of the bill, I observed the words of the Senator who introduced the bill. He said that confidence in trust companies is high in view of the character of the people in the industry; and secondly that there is further assurance of public protection through deposit insurance.
Speaking of trust companies, I am reminded of Prudential Trust, of British Mortgage and Trust, and some of the practices adopted by these companies. I also think of the lack of regulation and control by both federal and provincial governments at the time. I recall that when the matter was raised in this House the Minister of Finance said he had nothing to do with Prudential Trust, that it was a provincially incorporated company for which the provincial government was responsible. When one realizes that investors

in Prudential Trust will probably get a return of 10 cents on their investment dollar, is it any wonder that we need very close scrutiny and very close regulation at the federal level in regard to matters relating to trust companies? Again, this is why we contend that all financial institutions should come under the federal government's umbrella, and more particularly under the umbrella of the Bank of Canada.
I also recall the reluctance of financial institutions to accept the introduction of deposit insurance, and this gives me cause to smile at the Senator's statement that confidence is high now there is deposit insurance. May I call it four o'clock?

speechtext: Order. It being four o'clock the House will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business, as listed on today's order paper, namely, public bills.

that Bill C-16, to amend the Criminal Code (modernization of law of picketing), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-16 proposes an amendment to subsection 2 of section 366 of the Criminal Code of Canada. The purpose of the bill is to permit peaceful picketing by any number of people for the purpose not only of communicating information but of persuading other employees and people having business dealings with a company whose employees are on strike to support the cause of the picketers, particularly in the case of a lawful strike.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
At the present time section 366 of the Criminal Code prohibits intimidation by means of violence or threats, especially when conducted by watching or besetting. This is sensible. Subsection 2 of section 366 provides an exception in applying the concepts of watching or besetting. A person does not watch or beset, within the meaning of section 366, if he attends at or near or approaches a dwellinghouse or place only for the purpose of obtaining or communicating information.
December 12, 1969

As the law now reads, there are two significant defects in it. The first is that a judge in our courts may reasonably decide that in the case of an otherwise legally conducted strike any number of pickets except one is a form of intimidation. Such judgments have in fact been made. The reason is that subsection 2 begins with the words "A person who attends at or near". My proposed amendment would remove the possibility of such a decision in the future by replacing the single "person" with the plural "persons". With this change there would be no ambiguity in respect of the number of persons permitted to picket.
The second flaw in subsection 2 as it now reads is that it asserts that one does not watch or beset if one's purpose is only to obtain or communicate information. The legal force of this subsection is that if a man on strike, in addition to imparting information seeks actively to persuade others to follow his example, he can be charged with watching or besetting. My proposed revision of subsection 2 would make it a legitimate purpose of picketing to persuade or attempt to persuade, without violence or attempts at violence, others to do or not to do something.
Briefly, what are the arguments for this bill? One argument in favour of the change I am proposing is that it would give workers in Canada the same rights as other people in demonstrating for or against a cause they believe to be either just or unjust. It would make clear beyond doubt that more than one person must be permitted to join a demonstration or picket line. I suggest that the law as it now stands is discriminatory towards workers because it leaves to the courts the decision whether more than one person could be considered to be intimidating in a strike or a picket line.
Canadian law as it now stands applies a standard to workers that is not applied to other citizens. Why should not 50, 100 or 200, whatever be the figure, working people be allowed to demonstrate on a picket line just as they can now in respect of any other kind of demonstration? We have had demonstrations in respect of Biafra, the Lord's Day Act and Viet Nam.
We have in this country no laws that refer to demonstrations of this sort. Why do we have them for working people? It seems to me obvious from our own liberal traditions that there is contradiction here which should be abolished in our Criminal Code. We must abolish this double standard, one for working people and another for citizens at large. All 21545-52
Criminal Code
that is needed is the application of the same legal standard which imposes non-violent, nonintimidating behaviour on citizens. We must remove discriminatory legislation which sets our workers apart from other citizens in respect of their demonstrating. If there is violence and intimidation by workers on a picket line, of course they should be punished according to the laws of the land.
I am arguing that we should not have one set of laws for this kind of demonstration and another set of laws for others. Workers are citizens and they should have the same rights. They should be allowed to demonstrate in whatever numbers they decide is useful, just as other groups are allowed to demonstrate in a peaceful way in whatever number they are able to muster. Numbers do cause people to think; they sit back and reflect upon action taken and decide whether it is just. There is no reason, therefore, why a picket line or any other kind of demonstration should be arbitrarily restricted to one person.
The second improvement my amendment would make is that it would allow working people not only to communicate information, as is the case under the present law, but to actively persuade others that their cause is just. It would permit secondary picketing; it would permit workers to go virtually anywhere in the community and make their views known by means of a demonstration and carefully constructed arguments seeking public support for their activities.
I ask again, is this not an elementary freedom that the rest of us take for granted in our society? Whether one is for or against the war in Viet Nam, for or against Canadian involvement in the Nigeria-Biafra civil war, we do not impose restrictions on people demonstrating and distributing factual information. We look upon it as a right, and indeed a duty, for people to actively seek to persuade others of the justice of their cause.
Once again, 1 think the same rights should be given to working people who are seeking support for a cause in which they believe. They should have the right, therefore, not simply to give out factual information but to actively persuade members of the community to follow their example. I stress that if violence or intimidation of any sort should occur as a result of this activity, there should not be any legal exemption in respect of working people, just as there is not for people taking part in any other kind of demonstration. The same kind of standards

December 12, 1969
Criminal Code
should apply. Where the law is broken and where there is intimidation or violence, those involved should be punished.
That, very briefly, is my argument in favour of the bill. I am indebted to the Hon. Sidney Green, Minister of Health and Social Services in the Manitoba government, for the general framework of my argument. He argued along similar lines in that legislature in January, February and March of 1967. Those who want to be very well informed on this question should look at his arguments as well as the arguments of those who were opposed.
As I see it, the arguments I have put forward are clear and convincing to anyone in a liberal, democratic society. I look forward to hearing from those who intend to speak on this bill, especially those who intend to oppose it. 1 hope they will come to grips with these arguments and not go off on some other tack simply to talk the bill out. I present this challenge to them: Do they think that the workers of our country should have the same rights as other citizens, or are they in favour of discriminatory laws?

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the hon. member whether he admits that workers, apart from picketing, have the same rights as other citizens to parade and have people join their parade; to effect a demonstration similar to those for or against the Viet Nam war? Do the workers not have the right to parade that other citizens enjoy?

Yes, but with respect, as one says around here, I think the point has been missed. Of course workers have the same right if they want to demonstrate for or against the war in Viet Nam.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The point I am making is that picketing should be termed a demonstration much like other demonstrations, so that the same criteria in respect of violence, and so on, would hold for picketing as for other demonstrations. We should not have separate laws for different types of demonstrations; we should have the same law for all.

Mr. Speaker, I think if we examine the true meaning of picketing it will become obvious that the change in the Criminal Code suggested today is undesirable. Robert's Dictionary of Industrial Relations, the 1966 edition, defines picketing as "the actual patrolling at or near the employer's place of

business during a strike or other dispute, to give notice of the existence of a labour dispute, to publicize it, or to persuade workers to join the union, and to discourage or prevent persons from entering or going to work".
I am opposed to mass picketing because it goes beyond the purpose and creates dangerous side-effects conducive to inciting criminal conduct and infringing individual freedom. It also inhibits rational persuasion. The proposed bill is a reactionary suggestion which, if passed, would cause industrial relations to move backward rather than forward. I suggest that mass picketing would lead to competing picket lines, with the risk of physical violence. Today we should seek an end of the strike as a means of settling industrial disputes.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

I would be glad to do so at the end of my speech. We seek a change in the mode of operation. The meeting of violent competing groups is an anachronistic, costly method of settling industrial disputes. It is not the type of system we are trying to encourage. We are trying to get away from mass confrontation and to the point where we can reason out these matteris behind the table, along the line followed in Swedish industrial relations where they do not have a strike from one year to the other. I suggest the worst way to promote industrial harmony is to pass a law which encourages assemblies of those with competing views on the streets of our great cities and industrial centres. When we have a large corps of people in large centres, I suggest the worst way of settling their arguments is by shouting at each other in the streets. I suggest this is not in the interest of labour and that labour should not be represented by the fistswinging in the alley.
These things are portrayed on television. It hurts the cause of labour when people see an act of brutality like a car turned over or people being pushed around and bullied by irresponsible elements in the labour movement who do not adequately reflect the views of the clean-cut, fine Canadian union worker. I believe that patient negotiation with modern methods of conciliation is preferable to the average industrial worker in Canada today, rather than the assembly of large numbers on the picket lines. This view is based on information I have obtained in my riding from talking to industrial workers in Hamilton. A good many of them are
December 12, 1969

fed up with strikes and hope there will never be another one like the last one which, because of pressures from the United States, was distorted. I hope we will see a straightening-out and a balancing of the situation.
I believe that patient negotiation is preferable and that the industrial worker does not want to lose three or four months employment during a year because of a strike.
The assembly of large numbers of people on picket lines where there are competing groups is an example of a strike of the worst type. Certainly the results of crowd action in some cases are not because of the strike but because of lack of respect for the individual rights of citizens of this country. There have been examples of lawlessness and assaults which have been unrelated to a strike. I think this is a situation which should be watched today.
I believe in picketing. I advocate the cause of labour, the everlasting need to assure industrial workers of income and security protection. I also believe that much harm is done by the competition created by competing crowds angrily confronting each other on the street. The result is inevitable. There are assaults, threats, damage to property, overturned cars and disrespect for civil law and the police. Let us not forget the police. I suggest that representative picketing is much more effective than coercive, mass picketing in the cause of labour relations. I believe public opinion is against the type of activity which creates an atmosphere of tension and danger.
I should like to quote from Reynolds "Labour Economics and Labour Relations" at page 277:
Physical violence of any sort is unlawful. The pickets may not beat up strikebreakers, injure their cars or cause them other physical harm. By the same token strikebreakers and company police must not assault the strikers, spray them with tear gas or cause them physical damage.
I believe the bill presented today would tend to support violence and civil disorder. Once again I should like to read a quotation; it is taken from the 1966 report of the Ontario Royal Commission on Labour Disputes:
Mass picketing by relatively large numbers in close ranks or in group formation, effective generally in obstructing entrances to plants or businesses, is not lawful in any western country.
The word "mass" in this context means potential intimidation and mob rule through coercion and fear, the use of the implied threat, which causes the destruction of security and freedom for the ordinary citizen. If 21545-521
Criminal Code
we are interested in the maintenance of law and order, we will not permit the erosion of controlling criminals in the field of watching and besetting. The advocacy of threatening intimidation must be curbed in the interest of preserving state control. If it is not, we shall end up with lawlessness and violence, which is desired by only the most primitive people. The evidence indicates that picket line advocacy is on the decline. The trend is toward less provocative means of persuasion.
You would like to have it that way.

Yes. I think we should find more effective ways than we now have. You want to go back to the reactionary methods of primitive people who use this type of threat.
The necessarily incidental invasion of individual privacy and the private rights of citizens, caused by mass picketing, are ends which society must restrain in order to obtain a just society by means of legal methods.
What is a just society?

It is a society in which the people on two sides can sit down and negotiate together in good faith so that both sides can continue their economic development without losing time from work and being unemployed. That is what I mean by a just society. It is what we are striving to achieve, and we are moving in this direction rather than in the reactionary one of one mob confronting another. That will hot work.
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that violence at picket lines has frequently caused lasting bitterness and misunderstanding between individual citizens, as well as physical injury. This must stop. The present law regarding watching and besetting provides protection for the individual Canadian from the destruction of his right to come and go from place to place and to live without fear, apprehension or annoying inconvenience. I support the law as it now stands.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at great length on this proposed amendment. I hear someone say "Hear, hear". I feel very disappointed that someone may not be interested in hearing what I have to say. I see it was the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), my old friend "Smiling Jack".

[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I wish to commend the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) for bringing in this amendment. He said in his opening remarks that he was only asking for the same rights as others. He went on to say that if anyone broke the law, he should be charged and brought to court, the same as anyone else. I do not think workers should be set apart and dealt with differently than people in the medical profession, the legal profession or any other group. I do not know why so many people seem to think that workers who belong to a union are a strange breed of people, that they are ready to fight all the time. I do not think that is the case. There are some very intelligent men in the unions. The hon. member who introduced the amendment went on to say that there is a lack of communication between workers and members of the public and perhaps this could be overcome by way of pamphlets or any other means that are non-violent.
There is room for dissent in this country, there is room for parades and demonstrations, but there is definitely no room for violence. It is strange, but violence can be found among people in any branch of society. You will find violence even among the jovial cabinet members who smile so much. At times they get cross, as do humble Members of Parliament. So do members of any organization, fraternity or group in society become cross. I am sure there are times when anybody will lose his temper and become a little violent. But I do not think that a worker who is a member of a union is more prone to violence than anyone else.
We hear so much about equality of opportunity. This is thrown at us by the propaganda machinery of the present administration. We hear much about participatory democracy, the just society, and all these high-faluting phrases which do not mean a damn thing as far as I am concerned. The Prime Minister's office and the Privy Council office are being expanded tremendously. They are doing nothing but political work and they are not interested in what is happening in the country. Their sole purpose is to keep this administration in power, and they have their hands full with that. We have had a few months of "pretty Pierre," and God knows what kind of a mess the country will be in when he is defeated in four years' time.
The hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Gibson) gave us a very clear interpretation of picketing. He even told us where to

find it. That is very good; I am glad he knows what picketing means. He said he is opposed to mass picketing. He said it inhibits rational thinking and is a move backward rather than forward. He said he seeks an end to strikes, but he does not spell out the method. He says we will achieve a just society by sitting down and talking. He is looking for the millenium. He will find it as soon as he finds the just society, but he is not going to find a just society under this administration.
He wants to get away from mass confrontation and says that labour does not show the mailed fist. Then he speaks about workers and says what wonderful guys they are. He can speak so well out of both sides of his mouth that I think he is a candidate for the honour of having the greatest forked-tongue. He is doing a tremendous job in that field. He believes in picketing after damning everything pertaining to it. I ask whether he has ever in his short lifespan worked for a company or corporation with which a legitimately regulated union, approved by the law, tried to negotiate for months and in the meantime every effort was made by the company to destroy the rights of the workers in sneaky and underhanded ways, avoiding negotiation with reference to wages and hours of work, pensions, etc.
Has the hon. member ever worked for small wages, especially during the great days of the Liberal administration under Mackenzie King, when everyone was without a job until a guy named Hitler got them a job in September, 1939, and the Liberal administration took credit for it? Has he gone to the point where there was no alternative but to strike? That is the only thing that makes some people sit up and take notice.
Has he ever been on picket duty? Has he had a wife and children who had not much money because the company would not agree to negotiating with regard to proper living wages for its workers? I have been on strike, and I did not engage in violence. I played my part in the demonstrations, as a member of the union, and found this was the only way in which a decision could be reached after a long period of time. No one wants violence; no one wants war; no one wants the Viet Nam war-but regrettably it goes on. I was not lucky enough to have my father survive and send me to the best schools, and all that sort of thing, and look after me. I had to get out and work.

many months, not as the result of a picketline problem but as the result of being very badly smashed up in the coal mines. I could not serve, no matter how big I may look. speechtext:
The
hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Gibson) wants to ask a question of the hon. member.

I have heard it suggested that increased picketing would not endanger the situation, and that if there is violence the court can order that there be no more picketing. But is that not a little late when somebody's car has been upturned, when somebody has been beaten up, when somebody's leg has been broken and windows have been smashed in a few houses? Is that not too late to get a court order? Is there not some alternative way in which the law could act to alleviate the damage now caused? I throw this out to the hon. member to comment on its merits.

The
hon. member has thrown it to me. I was never a very good baseball player, but I have caught it. He is putting the same connotation on all members of a union no matter who they are. Some of the finest, upstanding citizens of this country are involved in unions. They are not only involved in the church, or

in the law society. You will find harum-scarums in those organizations, just as you do in unions.
Especially from around Renfrew.

Very much so. So I answer the hon. member by saying he is making a blanket criticism of all members of all unions, and I say God help society in this country and in other countries if we did not have unions. Next thing we know the hon. member will be saying he is against unions, that men should not be allowed to organize in order to fight for their rights and to negotiate for them.
I think the hon. member is wrong in thinking these are the only members of society who engage in violence or condone it. That is not right. He is committing a grave injustice when he speaks for the Liberal party and says that. He speaks for the Liberal party, as he did a moment ago.
You have not answered the problem with respect to the man with the overturned car or the broken window. You did not answer that.
This bill should now go to a vote, Mr. Speaker.
Question.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to express my opinion on the bill now before the House.
Bill C-16 is not new in this house. It seems to me that our friends of the New Democratic party should resort more often to that faculty we all have to various degrees, depending on our personality, which is known as imagination.
This bill was considered during the previous session and it seems to me that, quite frankly, it should have been introduced again under a different wording, instead of always using the same terms, without even changing its terminology.
The object of this bill, as previous speakers have said, is to permit peaceful picketing by any number for the purpose not only of communicating information but also of persuading other employees and people having business dealings with a struck company to support the cause of the picketers in the case, particularly, of a lawful strike.
It seems to me that, under our present legislation, whether at the provincial or the federal level, every Canadian can freely enjoy the privilege of engaging in a number of activities whenever there is picketing during a strike. As most members here, I am honestly doing my best to defend the rights of our Canadian workers. While I certainly intend, together with the other Liberal members, to go on doing whatever I can to improve their condition, I cannot help wondering why the sponsor of the bill wants to give the impression that he is their only true champion in the House. There is something rather biased in this approach.
That is true.

Earlier, the hon. member jumped on the opportunity to put forward some opinions which I think irrelevant to the subject. He even mentioned demonstrations in Biafra. I wonder in which way our behaviour toward Biafra could at all help the Canadian workers. He says demonstrations are non-violent, with a few rare exceptions. I am sure the majority of Canadians or, at least, all the members of the House, are against violent demonstrations.
Why should anybody come here to talk about great principles and suggest that some
Criminal Code
political party might be in favour of violent demonstrations? One of the primary principles of the Liberal party is the respect of true freedom.
In Canada, this country we love so much, most citizens prefer to live in peace. For many years, we have been in that an example to the world. Indeed, the Canadian people have shown they wish to live in peace among themselves and with the rest of the world.
As regards the communication of information to the public by the workers, the latter have at their disposal the same means as those made available to members of parliament and other citizens to supply information. We must strive to provide reporters and other persons involved in the information field, accurate information, while not forgetting peace, goodwill and the improvement of the social or economic level we are all striving for.
The sponsor of this bill even managed to talk about the war in Viet Nam. I know there are workers and private citizens in Viet Nam, whom we must protect and assist, but it seemed to me, as he made us fly over the seas to take us to Viet Nam, that he was wandering quite a bit from the problem concerning the Canadian workers. He resorted to insinuation methods of which I and many other Canadians do not approve.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Is it possible to find in Canada, with certain exceptions, a right-thinking person who would be for the war in Viet Nam?
These are what I call misrepresentations which do not serve the Canadian workers at all. Since we are talking about freedom, I think I am relevant in view of the fact that in Canada, as in most other countries, a group of workers exercise its right to freedom by going on strike. Here again, at every level, freedom is being misrepresented.
Everyone considers himself an expert philosopher, which allows him to give his own definition of freedom and I must humbly admit that I am no more an expert than the others in this field but I do believe that the principle of freedom must not be based on emotions, feelings or instinct in general, but on reason. This is why I think freedom cannot exist without order. This is an old saying often heard in our circles.
As I said before, I think that the Canadian workers enjoy the same rights as others, and we get more evidence of this all the time. I know that, especially in the province of Quebec, almost every day something happens

December 12, 1969
Criminal Code
to prove that, as all the other classes of society in Canada, the workers take advantage of their right to picket lines and public demonstrations. In fact, we must recognize honestly that this right to hold public demonstrations is often abused and when a right is abused, in the name of individual or collective freedom, there is interference with the freedom of others.
This is why, in Canada, we fear massive picketings. I would not say that we oppose them, but we fear them because when they aim at protecting the freedom of one group, they can interfere with the freedom of others. And even if one speaks of the intelligence of labour leaders-I have friends among labour leaders, as most of us, by the way-many of them are very intelligent but in other respects, they are also human beings who have the right of association. But other interests can also be involved within their group, as those which the sponsor of this bill may have. Whether political or otherwise, those interests may sometimes conflict with those of the labourer or of the worker.
We have very intelligent leaders, but there are some who do not show any sense of responsibility but rather a sense of irresponsibility and use the means at their disposal, which are quite valid in principle, in order to intimidate the masses.
By appealing not to reason, rational understanding or common sense but rather to passions and instincts we interfere with freedom which we all want to enjoy.
Like the government and right-minded Canadian citizens did and continue to do we must unite in order to find the less irritating ways to solve the problems which are facing Canadian workers and all other Canadians.
I speak the truth when I say that some strikers, not to say many, have created quite a lot more problems than they have solved.
Question.

Mr. Speaker, I am dealing with the subject. I remember the
words of the sponsor of this bill last year when he spoke of evasion and intimidation. Apparently, he was accusing the government by implying that it was resorting to tactics of intimidation and evasion with the Canadian people.
I think that the hon. member himself is using evasion and intimidation because, each year, he sponsors the same bill in order to be known as one of the great defenders of Canadian workers. I do not agree with that.
He spoke of non-violent persuasion, yet he introduces this bill by saying that we must make every effort to improve the system of picketing in Canada, whereas we probably enjoy the best system in the world.
According to him, to see several pickets is an impressive show. I know that it is always moving to see a group of human beings sincerely trying to solve their problems. It is for the same reason that it is impressive to work altogether in the House in order to settle the difficulties faced by workers and make the best suggestions possible to the government of Canada, of which we are proud, so that it will be as efficient as it can be.
To my way of thinking, the problems of the Canadian worker cannot be solved in 30 seconds or an hour. It is, however, possible to improve the picketing situation.
